assumptions: Accredited laboratories continue to own sampling and issuance of raw results, while a competent water-safety professional owns interpretation and escalation rules.
A single Polish laboratory integration can be piloted within the stated capital and part-time constraints, but no partner commitment or outcome-data right is assumed.
Per-sample pricing, portfolio pricing, margins, volumes, and connector costs remain unvalidated planning assumptions.
Cross-building comparisons are used only where system characteristics, sampling protocols, interventions, and follow-up outcomes are sufficiently comparable.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Recurring regulated testing creates a natural event at which contextual trend and remediation support could be delivered. The potentially valuable insight is to close the loop from result through intervention and retest rather than merely display a sample, but existing portals already offer trends and dashboards and the benchmark thesis depends on richer context not yet available.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Disease risk, frequent poor hot-water results, and recurring compliance duties establish real customer pain. They do not establish incremental willingness to pay for analytics beyond accredited testing, existing laboratory reporting, specialist advice, and facility-management systems.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Per-sample revenue plus portfolio subscriptions could recur alongside scheduled tests and retests. The proposed prices, 100000-sample scale, laboratory share, expert-review burden, secure integration cost, margin, retention, and payback are all unobserved, and a laboratory may regard basic trend reporting as a bundled feature rather than a separately monetizable product.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish healthcare, lodging, care, and multi-site property portfolios provide a clear regulated beachhead, and later geographic or testing-category expansion is possible. The supplied evidence establishes testing activity and exceedances but not the number of reachable paying portfolios or enough volume to support the planning case.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Eurofins and LegionellaDossier already market trend analytics, dashboards, and non-compliance management. An embedded laboratory partnership could create local access, but the laboratory controls the channel and can bundle or internalize the capability; no exclusive data or distribution position is evidenced.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A validated closed-loop model could extend across building classes, geographies, other water risks, environmental tests, and portfolio risk management. Expansion would require jurisdiction-specific guidance, comparable covariates, and further lab integrations, so it is plausible but not automatic.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Contractually reusable intervention and retest outcomes could create a differentiated longitudinal dataset and workflow switching costs. Data rights are unknown, sampling is sparse and heterogeneous, and the laboratory or incumbent platform may possess both the source data and customer relationship, leaving the proposed analytics layer structurally vulnerable.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Comparable-building evidence and closed-loop remediation analysis could be more actionable than a result portal. Its validity and decision impact are unproved, while official guidance emphasizes that samples can misrepresent system risk and require expert, system-specific interpretation, constraining any generalized benchmark advantage.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: EU and Polish risk-management duties, recent reported exceedances, and a rising disease notification rate create continuing attention and recurring work. The need and analytics category are not new, and the evidence does not show a regulatory change that uniquely favors this entrant now.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: An accredited lab can expose the product at the recurring testing event and distribute it across many operator accounts, which is more efficient than direct facility sales. No laboratory has committed to integration, margin sharing, resale, or data rights, and dependence on a small number of powerful channel owners creates substantial hold-up risk.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The analytics work fits the founder and outsourced sampling keeps the model asset-light. Reliable deployment still requires laboratory integration, expert governance, liability controls, secure data handling, sufficient covariates, and careful avoidance of false reassurance; a narrow pilot is feasible, but production-grade credibility is materially harder.

main_structural_strength: The product can attach to a mandatory recurring sampling event through a concentrated accredited-laboratory channel, creating repeat usage without owning physical sampling operations.
primary_score_limiter: The proposed differentiated value and moat both depend on obtaining comparable building, intervention, and retest data from laboratory partners, yet rights, density, validity, incremental willingness to pay, and partner economics are all unknown.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Existing laboratory and specialist vendors already provide trend analytics and compliance dashboards, while official guidance states that samples alone can miss system risk and require competent contextual interpretation, undermining a generic analytics add-on.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A paid laboratory pilot should contractually secure intervention and retest rights for a homogeneous property cohort, demonstrate expert-validated benchmark reliability and changed control decisions, obtain renewals from portfolio operators, and show positive contribution after integration, channel share, review, support, and insurance costs.
highest_value_structural_change: Narrow the first product to one comparable building class and own a standardized closed-loop remediation protocol from positive result through documented intervention and retest, rather than offering broad cross-building dashboards; this would improve validity, actionability, and the chance of proprietary outcome data.
